section: Compliance, Privacy, and Security for Storage
title: Compliance isn't paperwork: it's hard storage requirements
body: Many engineers see compliance as lawyer paperwork. That is wrong. Laws and audits create hard technical requirements for storage: where bytes may physically live, who may read them, how long they must be kept, how fast they must be deleted, and how you prove all of it. Some of the biggest storage projects at Meta, Google, and Microsoft in the last ten years were driven by privacy law, not by performance or cost. Almost every storage decision now has a legal side.
deeper:
The chapter follows a running example: a global app with 1 billion users. It stores profiles (personal data), photos and videos, messages (sensitive), logs and events (full of user IDs and IP addresses), and an analytics lake that holds copies of everything. Each of these stores carries a different legal burden. Profiles and messages fall under privacy law's access and erasure rights. Logs look harmless but are packed with identifiers, so they count as personal data too. The analytics lake is the trap: it is a copy of everything, so every obligation that applies to the originals also applies there.

The chapter first explains the rules in plain language, then shows how storage systems implement them: encryption and key management, deletion at scale, retention and WORM (write once, read many), access control and audit logs, data discovery, and finally the organizations and platforms that tie it all together. The goal is to know which technical capability each rule forces you to build, not to memorize legal text.

quiz.q: Why does the analytics lake in the running example carry the same legal burden as the primary stores?
quiz.a: Because it holds copies of everything, including personal data. Every obligation on the originals, such as erasure, access, and residency, applies to every copy too.

section: Compliance, Privacy, and Security for Storage
title: Privacy is cross-cutting: one delete touches every copy
body: A delete request touches every system that ever copied the user's data: databases, blob stores, caches, logs, indexes, analytics tables, and backups. That is why privacy requirements cannot be solved inside one storage service. They need platform-level building blocks shared across the company: identity on every record, lineage showing where data flowed, encryption keys per user or per dataset, and a central deletion framework. Without these, each team reinvents partial solutions and data leaks through the gaps.
deeper:
This is the senior staff view of the whole chapter. Each building block maps to a later section. Identity on every record means every row, event, and file carries the user ID it belongs to, so you can find it for an access or erasure request. Lineage means the platform records that a job read table A and wrote table B, which is how you build a data map that stays current. Keys per user or per dataset enable crypto-shredding: delete one key and every copy encrypted with it, including backups, becomes unreadable. A central deletion framework, like Meta's DELF, fans out a single request to every store and verifies completion.

The pitfall is treating privacy as a feature of one service. A perfectly compliant profile database is useless if the same data sits in a Kafka topic, a search index, and an ML training set that nobody wired into deletion. Cross-cutting problems need cross-cutting infrastructure, owned at the platform level rather than by each product team.

quiz.q: Why can't a single storage team solve GDPR erasure inside its own service?
quiz.a: User data is copied into many systems (caches, logs, indexes, lakes, backups). Erasure needs platform-wide identity, lineage, per-user keys, and a central deletion framework that reaches every copy.

title: GDPR: global reach, 4% of turnover fines
body: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has applied since May 2018. It covers personal data: any information about an identifiable person, including user IDs, IP addresses, and device IDs, not just names and emails. It applies to any company that offers services to people in the EU, wherever the company is based. Fines can reach 20 million euros or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher. For large tech companies, the turnover-based cap makes GDPR a board-level risk.
deeper:
The broad definition of personal data is what makes GDPR a storage problem. If IP addresses and device IDs count, then request logs, clickstream events, CDN logs, and analytics tables are all in scope, not just the user profile table. That is why the running example's logs are called 'full of user IDs and IP addresses': they carry the same obligations as the profile store.

The extraterritorial reach matters too. A US company with no EU office still falls under GDPR if it serves people in the EU. So a global app with a billion users cannot avoid it by where it incorporates or where its data centers sit.

The fine structure, the higher of 20 million euros or 4% of global annual turnover, means the penalty scales with company size. For the biggest firms, 4% of turnover is billions. That is what turned privacy law into a driver of major infrastructure projects at Meta, Google, and Microsoft, on par with performance and cost.

quiz.q: Why does GDPR's definition of personal data pull request logs and analytics tables into scope?
quiz.a: Personal data includes any identifier of a person, such as user IDs, IP addresses, and device IDs. Logs and analytics tables are full of these, so they carry the same obligations.

title: GDPR access and erasure: automate or drown
body: Two GDPR rights shape storage most. The right of access (Article 15) lets a person get a copy of their data, so storage must find all data for one user across all systems. The right to erasure (Article 17) lets a person ask you to delete their data, so storage must delete one user's data everywhere, including copies. Companies must answer these requests within one month, extendable in some cases. At a billion users, that means fully automated pipelines, not engineers running scripts.
deeper:
The storage consequences are concrete. Access requires that every store can be queried by user ID, which in turn requires that every record carries a user identity and that you know which stores exist (a data map). Export then has to gather results from profile databases, blob stores, message stores, logs, and derived datasets into one package.

Erasure is harder, because it must reach replicas, caches, indexes, logs, analytics copies, ML training sets, and backups, not just the primary row. The chapter later treats this as one of the hardest distributed-systems problems at a big company.

The one-month deadline is what forces automation. With a billion users, even a tiny fraction making requests each month produces a steady stream of work. Manual handling does not scale and is error-prone: a missed table means data left behind, a wrong query means deleting the wrong data. Mature companies therefore build self-service export tools and central deletion frameworks that run these requests end to end and record completion as evidence for auditors.

quiz.q: Why does the one-month GDPR deadline force automation for a billion-user system?
quiz.a: Request volume at that scale is continuous, and each request must search or delete across every store. Manual scripts can't keep up reliably, so access and erasure must be automated pipelines.

title: GDPR's other storage rules: minimize, expire, secure, locate
body: Beyond access and erasure, GDPR has five more principles that hit storage. Data minimization (Article 5): collect only what you need, so drop unneeded fields and set TTLs. Storage limitation (Article 5): don't keep data longer than needed, so use automatic expiry and lifecycle rules. Security of processing (Article 32): encryption, access control, logging. Breach notification (Article 33): tell the regulator within 72 hours. Transfers (Chapter V): limits on moving data outside the EU, so you must know and control location.
deeper:
Each principle turns into a platform feature. Minimization and storage limitation become retention limits, per-table TTLs, lifecycle rules on buckets, and schema reviews that reject fields nobody needs. These features also reduce cost and blast radius: data you never kept cannot leak and never needs deleting.

Security of processing is deliberately vague ('appropriate measures'), but in practice auditors expect encryption at rest and in transit, least-privilege access, and logging.

The 72-hour breach notification rule is where logging becomes critical. To notify responsibly you must know what was accessed. If object-level access logs were never enabled, you cannot prove what was or was not read, and lawyers often assume the worst, which means notifying every possibly affected user.

The transfers rule in Chapter V is the root of the data residency work covered next: if you cannot say where every copy of EU personal data lives, including metadata, logs, and backups, you cannot show that transfers had a legal basis.

quiz.q: How does GDPR's 72-hour breach notification rule create a storage requirement?
quiz.a: You must quickly determine what data was accessed. That requires audit logs detailed enough, like object-level data-event logs, to show who read what.

title: Schrems II: the court that killed Privacy Shield
body: GDPR allows transfers of personal data outside the EU only with safeguards. For years, many US companies relied on the EU-US Privacy Shield. In July 2020, the Court of Justice of the EU invalidated it in the Schrems II case, because of US government surveillance powers. Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs), contract terms between sender and receiver, stayed valid, but only with 'supplementary measures' when the destination country's law does not give equal protection. Overnight, a common legal basis for storing EU data in the US disappeared.
deeper:
Schrems II showed that the legal ground under an architecture can move. Companies that had built global storage systems, with EU user data replicated freely into US regions, suddenly depended on SCCs plus supplementary measures, which regulators could still challenge. Supplementary measures in practice often mean technical protections such as strong encryption where keys stay under the exporter's control, so the data is unintelligible to anyone in the destination country.

This ruling is a key reason why keeping EU data in the EU became an engineering goal rather than just a legal preference. It also links directly to key-control features covered later in the chapter: customer-managed keys and hold-your-own-key setups are ways to argue that even if bytes sit abroad, they cannot be read there.

For storage engineers, the lesson is that transfer mechanisms are legal constructs that courts can strike down, while data location is something you control in your own system. Designing for location control is the more durable bet.

quiz.q: Why did Schrems II push companies to keep EU data physically in the EU?
quiz.a: It invalidated Privacy Shield and made SCC transfers depend on extra measures. Transfer mechanisms proved legally fragile, so controlling data location became the safer architectural choice.

title: Meta's 1.2 billion euro fine for storing EU data in the US
body: In May 2023, the Irish Data Protection Commission fined Meta 1.2 billion euros for transferring EU users' Facebook data to the US under Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs). It also ordered Meta to stop the transfers and to stop storing that data in the US. It is the largest GDPR fine so far. The case shows that where your bytes sit is not only an infrastructure detail: a storage placement decision can produce a billion-euro penalty and an order to move data.
deeper:
This fine came after Schrems II had already invalidated the Privacy Shield in July 2020. Meta had continued transfers under SCCs, and the regulator found that was not enough given US surveillance law. The two-part order is what makes it a storage story. Paying a fine is a finance problem; being ordered to stop storing data in a country is an infrastructure problem, because it can require relocating or deleting huge datasets, reworking replication, and changing which regions serve which users.

For an architect, the case is the strongest argument for regional partitioning built in from the start. If each user has a home region and personal data stays there, a change in transfer law is a legal update, not a multi-year migration. The key takeaways of the chapter highlight this sequence, Schrems II in 2020, Meta's fine in 2023, and the new Data Privacy Framework in 2023, as evidence that cross-border rules are unstable and should not be the foundation of your design.

quiz.q: Why is the 2023 Meta fine more than a financial event for storage teams?
quiz.a: Besides 1.2 billion euros, Meta was ordered to stop transfers and stop storing EU data in the US. That forces data relocation and replication changes, an infrastructure problem.

title: Data Privacy Framework: transfers are back, trust is not
body: In July 2023, the European Commission adopted an adequacy decision for the new EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF). It again allows transfers of personal data to US companies that certify under it. Legally, this reopened a simple path for EU-to-US data flows. But many companies no longer bet their architecture on a transfer mechanism that courts may strike down again, as they did with Privacy Shield. They build the ability to keep EU data in the EU anyway.
deeper:
The history explains the caution. Privacy Shield was invalidated in July 2020 by Schrems II. SCCs survived but were weakened, and Meta was fined 1.2 billion euros in May 2023 for relying on them. Only two months later, the DPF arrived. A mechanism that can appear and disappear within a few years is a poor foundation for a storage system whose data might live for a decade.

So the pragmatic design is dual: use the DPF where it helps, but keep the technical ability to confine EU personal data to EU regions if the legal ground shifts again. For the chapter's running app, this becomes regional partitioning, where each user has a home region for personal data, and cross-region services see only pseudonymized or aggregated data.

The broader principle is that legal mechanisms are volatile while architecture is slow to change. Building location control once is cheaper than re-architecting each time a court rules.

quiz.q: If the DPF allows EU-US transfers again, why do companies still build EU-only data storage?
quiz.a: Courts struck down the previous mechanism and may do so again. Keeping the ability to confine EU data to the EU protects the architecture from legal reversals.

title: CCPA/CPRA: California's delete rights plus opt-out flags
body: The California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) took effect in January 2020. The California Privacy Rights Act (CPRA) amended it, with most changes effective January 2023, and created a dedicated regulator, the California Privacy Protection Agency. Consumers can know, delete, and correct their data, and opt out of its 'sale' or 'sharing'. Businesses generally have 45 days to respond. Technically, CCPA needs the same find, export, and delete capabilities as GDPR, plus opt-out flags that travel with data downstream.
deeper:
The opt-out flag is the part that is new relative to GDPR. When a user opts out of sale or sharing, that choice must reach every downstream system that might use the data for those purposes, especially ads and analytics. A flag stored only in the profile database is not enough if the ads pipeline reads a copy of events from a lake that never learned about the opt-out. So the flag must be propagated along with the data, or checked at the point of use.

This is a preview of purpose-based controls later in the chapter, such as Meta's Policy Zones, where labels on data travel with it through jobs and block disallowed uses.

The response windows differ: GDPR allows one month, CCPA generally 45 days. A company serving both groups usually builds one deletion and export platform that meets the tighter deadline, rather than separate systems per law. The shared building blocks are the same: identity on records, a data map, and automated fan-out of requests.

quiz.q: What does CCPA require technically that goes beyond GDPR-style find and delete?
quiz.a: Opt-out flags for sale or sharing that travel with the data to downstream systems like ads and analytics, so every copy respects the user's choice.

title: HIPAA: encryption is optional on paper, universal in practice
body: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Security Rule protects electronic protected health information (PHI). It requires administrative, physical, and technical safeguards: access control, audit controls, integrity, and transmission security. Encryption is formally 'addressable', meaning you must implement it or document why an alternative is equivalent. But in practice everyone encrypts, because HHS guidance treats properly encrypted data as 'secured', so losing encrypted data does not trigger breach notification.
deeper:
The breach notification safe harbor is the economic lever. If a laptop or a disk with PHI is lost and the data was properly encrypted, the organization does not have to notify patients and regulators. If it was not encrypted, the same incident becomes a reportable breach, with investigations, notifications, and reputational damage. That makes encryption the cheap default even though the rule technically lets you argue for an alternative.

The four technical safeguard areas map directly onto storage features. Access control means least-privilege IAM on PHI stores. Audit controls mean logging who accessed which records. Integrity means protecting data from improper alteration, which ties back to checksums and data integrity work. Transmission security means TLS for data in transit.

The pattern, where encryption turns a leak into a non-event legally, recurs across the chapter: it is also part of why crypto-shredding and customer-managed keys are powerful, since unreadable data is treated very differently from readable data.

quiz.q: Why does nearly everyone encrypt PHI even though HIPAA calls encryption only 'addressable'?
quiz.a: HHS treats properly encrypted data as secured, so losing it doesn't trigger breach notification. Encryption turns a reportable breach into a non-event.

title: A secure service can still break HIPAA: the BAA list
body: Cloud providers that handle protected health information (PHI) sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with their customers. The BAA is the legal contract under HIPAA that makes the provider responsible for safeguarding PHI. Providers also publish which of their services are 'HIPAA eligible', meaning covered by that agreement. Using a non-eligible service to store PHI is a compliance failure, even if the service is technically secure. Compliance depends on the contract and scope, not only on encryption and access controls.
deeper:
This is a subtle trap for engineers. A team might pick a new managed database or logging product because it encrypts data and has good IAM, then pipe PHI into it. If that service is not on the provider's HIPAA-eligible list, the organization is out of compliance regardless of how secure the configuration is, because no BAA covers it.

The practical consequence is that data classification must drive service choice. If a dataset is labeled PHI, the platform should only allow it into eligible services. This fits the chapter's later theme that classification labels should drive controls automatically rather than rely on engineers remembering rules.

The same shape appears with other regimes. PCI DSS has an 'in scope' concept for systems that touch card data, and FedRAMP authorizes specific cloud services for federal use. In each case, the question is not just 'is this secure?' but 'is this service formally covered for this data type?'

quiz.q: A service encrypts data and has strong IAM. Why could storing PHI in it still violate HIPAA?
quiz.a: If it isn't on the provider's HIPAA-eligible list, it isn't covered by the Business Associate Agreement, so using it for PHI is a compliance failure regardless of security.

title: PCI DSS Requirement 3: never keep the CVV, hide the PAN
body: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) is an industry standard, not a law, but card networks enforce it. Version 4.0 was published in 2022, and its 'future-dated' requirements became mandatory on March 31, 2025. Requirement 3 covers stored account data: never store sensitive authentication data, like the CVV code, after authorization; make the primary account number (PAN) unreadable wherever stored, using strong encryption, truncation, hashing, or tokenization; and manage the keys carefully.
deeper:
Each rule has a storage implication. 'Never store the CVV after authorization' means payment flows must make sure the code does not end up in logs, message queues, error traces, or analytics events, which is where it usually leaks. A single debug log line that prints a full request body can put a company in violation.

'PAN unreadable wherever stored' applies to every copy: databases, backups, logs, and exports. The four options differ. Truncation keeps only some digits and cannot be reversed. Hashing is one-way. Encryption is reversible with the key, which makes key management part of the requirement. Tokenization replaces the PAN with a meaningless token and keeps the real number in a separate vault.

'Manage the keys carefully' ties PCI back to the encryption section: key storage, rotation, and separation of duties are audited. The phased rollout of version 4.0, published in 2022 with future-dated items mandatory from March 31, 2025, gave companies time to adapt their systems.

quiz.q: Where does a stored CVV typically sneak into a system despite PCI rules, and why does that matter?
quiz.a: In logs, queues, error traces, or analytics events that capture request bodies. PCI forbids storing it after authorization anywhere, so any such copy is a violation.

title: PCI scope reduction: one token vault, everything else out
body: Under PCI DSS, every system that stores or can reach card numbers is 'in scope' and must pass a strict audit. The most important storage pattern is therefore scope reduction. Companies store primary account numbers (PANs) in one small, isolated token vault and give every other system a token instead of the real number. The token is useless to an attacker and not card data. The rest of the storage fleet then stays out of scope, which shrinks audit cost and risk dramatically.
deeper:
The key word is 'can reach'. Scope is not only systems that hold card numbers but also systems with network paths or credentials to them. That is why the vault must be isolated: separate network, tight access, few callers. If a general analytics cluster could query the vault, it would be pulled into scope too.

With tokenization, order systems, customer support tools, analytics, and logs all work with tokens. When a real charge is needed, a narrow payment service asks the vault to detokenize. Only the vault and that path need the full PCI audit.

The benefits compound. Fewer in-scope systems means fewer controls to evidence, smaller blast radius if something is breached, and freedom for most engineering teams to use ordinary tools without PCI constraints. The same idea, concentrate sensitive data in a small hardened place and hand out references elsewhere, generalizes beyond payments and echoes the chapter's advice to pseudonymize data before it enters shared systems like an analytics lake.

quiz.q: How does a token vault reduce PCI DSS audit burden?
quiz.a: Only the isolated vault holds real PANs; other systems get tokens, which aren't card data. So only the vault and its narrow access path are in scope for the strict audit.

title: SOX: prove who changed financial data and code
body: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) of 2002 requires US public companies to maintain internal controls over financial reporting, under Section 404. For storage, that means auditable controls on who can change financial data and the code that processes it, how those changes are approved, and logs that prove it. SOX is less about encryption and more about change control and traceability: an auditor must be able to see that every change to financial systems was authorized and recorded.
deeper:
In practice, SOX touches storage through a few recurring controls. Access to financial databases and data warehouses must be limited to people with a business need, with periodic access reviews. Changes to schemas, pipelines, and code that feed financial reports must go through approval workflows, such as code review and change tickets. And there must be logs showing who did what and when, kept in a way that cannot be quietly edited.

This overlaps with what certification auditors look for in general: least privilege with regular access reviews, tamper-resistant logs, and traceable configuration changes. A company that already runs continuous compliance, with automated checks and system-collected evidence, finds SOX much easier than one that assembles screenshots once a year.

The storage pitfall is manual 'hotfixes' to financial data by engineers with broad database access. Even when correct, an unapproved and unlogged change is a control failure under SOX.

quiz.q: Why is an engineer's correct but unlogged manual fix to financial data still a SOX problem?
quiz.a: SOX requires controls showing changes to financial data and code are approved and logged. An unapproved, untraceable change is a control failure even if the result is right.

title: SEC 17a-4: WORM, the audit-trail option, and Object Lock
body: SEC Rule 17a-4 requires broker-dealers to keep certain records, like trades and communications, for set periods, often 3 or 6 years. Under paragraph (f), electronic records historically had to be stored in WORM format: write once, read many, meaning they cannot be changed or deleted before the retention period ends. In October 2022, the SEC amended the rule to also allow an audit-trail alternative: a system keeping a complete, time-stamped history of every change so the original can always be recreated.
deeper:
This rule is why cloud providers built compliance-grade immutability. Amazon S3 Object Lock was assessed by Cohasset Associates for use under SEC 17a-4, CFTC, and FINRA rules. Azure immutable blob storage and Google Cloud Storage Bucket Lock have similar assessments. An independent assessment matters because a regulated firm must show auditors that its storage truly enforces the rule, not just that it has a setting called 'lock'.

The two paths differ in design. WORM prevents change entirely during retention, even by admins. The 2022 audit-trail alternative allows changes but requires a complete, time-stamped history so that any original version can be rebuilt. Versioned storage with immutable logs can fit that model.

WORM directly conflicts with privacy-driven deletion, which the chapter handles later: regulatory retention and legal holds are recognized GDPR exceptions, and the system must support deleting everything else while keeping the held records until retention ends.

quiz.q: What did the October 2022 amendment to SEC Rule 17a-4 change for storage design?
quiz.a: Besides strict WORM, firms may use an audit-trail system that keeps a complete, time-stamped history of every change so the original record can always be recreated.

title: Residency vs sovereignty: location vs whose laws apply
body: Data residency means data must be stored in a particular country or region. Data sovereignty goes further: the data is subject only to the laws of that country, and ideally cannot be reached by foreign governments or even by the provider's staff abroad. Residency is about where the bytes sit; sovereignty is about who can legally and practically touch them. A bucket in Frankfurt satisfies residency, but if engineers in another country can read it, sovereignty is not achieved.
deeper:
Different jurisdictions push in different directions. The European Union has no strict localization rule under GDPR Chapter V and Schrems II, but transfers need a legal basis, so many companies keep EU data in the EU anyway. Russia, Vietnam, Indonesia, and others have various localization rules for specific data types.

Sovereignty adds operational requirements beyond location. Keys must be held in-jurisdiction, support staff must be local, metadata and logs must not leave, and the system should keep working if links abroad are cut. That is why cloud providers built separate sovereign offerings instead of just adding regions.

For architects, the distinction clarifies what to ask. A residency requirement is often satisfied by region pinning and replication rules. A sovereignty requirement also constrains operations, support access, key custody, and control-plane dependencies, which is a much larger design problem.

quiz.q: A company stores EU data in Frankfurt but US-based engineers can read it. Is that residency, sovereignty, or both?
quiz.a: Residency only. The bytes are in the right place, but sovereignty also requires that foreign staff and governments cannot reach the data.

title: India and China: negative lists and in-country storage
body: Two big jurisdictions shape storage placement. India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act 2023 allows transfers except to countries the government restricts, a 'negative list'. Rules notified in November 2025 phase in obligations through May 2027. Separately, the Reserve Bank of India has required payment system data to be stored only in India since 2018. China's Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL), effective November 2021, plus the Data Security Law, require critical infrastructure operators and large processors to store personal data in China.
deeper:
The contrast is useful. India's DPDP is permissive by default: data can flow abroad unless the destination is restricted. But a sector rule overrides this for payments: since 2018, the RBI requires payment system data to stay in India. So one company can face different rules for different data types in the same country, which means classification (knowing which data is payment data) directly drives placement.

China is stricter. Under PIPL, effective November 2021, together with the Data Security Law, critical infrastructure operators and large processors must store personal data in China, and exports need a security assessment or another approved mechanism.

The EU sits between: no strict localization, but transfers need a legal basis. The practical architecture for a global app is regional partitioning with per-data-type policies. Each user has a home region, and the platform knows which data classes can leave it, under which mechanism, and which cannot leave at all.

quiz.q: Why can one company face different data-location rules for different datasets in India?
quiz.a: DPDP generally allows transfers except to restricted countries, but RBI rules since 2018 require payment system data to stay in India. Data type decides placement.

title: Sovereign clouds: data, keys, metadata, and operators stay local
body: Cloud providers now sell sovereign cloud offerings. The AWS European Sovereign Cloud became generally available in January 2026, with its first region in Brandenburg, Germany. AWS describes it as physically and logically separate from other AWS Regions, operated only by EU residents located in the EU, and designed to keep running even if connectivity to the rest of the world is cut. Microsoft built the EU Data Boundary, and Google offers sovereign controls and partner-operated clouds, for example with Thales in France.
deeper:
The designs differ, but the common goal is that data, keys, metadata, and operators all stay inside the jurisdiction. Each element closes a different gap. Data residency alone is covered by ordinary regions. Keeping keys local means foreign staff cannot decrypt. Keeping metadata local matters because object names, tags, and control-plane records can contain personal data. Keeping operators local addresses the sovereignty concern that foreign employees could be compelled to provide access.

The AWS requirement to keep running with connectivity cut off is notable: it means the sovereign cloud cannot depend on a global control plane, identity service, or key service outside the EU. That is a significant engineering undertaking, not a configuration switch.

The partner-operated model, such as Google working with Thales in France, puts a local company in charge of operations, which strengthens the legal argument that the data sits under local law only. For customers, these offerings trade some features and cost for a much stronger sovereignty story.

quiz.q: Why does the AWS European Sovereign Cloud need to run even if cut off from the rest of the world?
quiz.a: True sovereignty means no dependency on control planes, identity, or keys outside the EU. If it needed foreign services to run, foreign parties could affect or reach the data.

title: Data in Frankfurt, debug logs in Virginia: residency leaks
body: Residency is not only about where the blobs are. It also covers metadata, since object names can contain email addresses; logs full of IPs and user IDs; backups; replicas used for disaster recovery; support access by engineers in other countries; and encryption keys. A common audit failure is 'data in Frankfurt, but the search index and the debug logs in Virginia.' Any copy or derivative of personal data outside the region can break the residency promise.
deeper:
This is a senior staff lens because the failures are almost always in secondary systems that nobody thinks of as storing user data. A search index built from EU documents contains their text. A tracing or debug log captures request payloads. A DR replica is set up in the cheapest distant region. A global metrics system tags samples with user IDs. Each of these quietly moves personal data abroad.

Keys are part of residency too. If the key that decrypts EU data lives in a key service in another country, or can be used by staff there, then the encrypted bytes in Frankfurt are effectively reachable from abroad.

The fix is to treat residency as a property of the data class, enforced everywhere the data flows, not as a property of one primary store. That requires lineage to know where copies go and organization-level guardrails, such as policies that forbid creating resources outside EU regions for EU workloads. The key takeaways repeat this: residency must include metadata, logs, backups, and keys.

quiz.q: Name three places EU personal data commonly leaks out of region despite the primary store being in the EU.
quiz.a: Search indexes, debug or request logs, and DR replicas or backups. Also metadata like object names, support access from abroad, and keys held elsewhere.

title: Home regions: keep personal data local, share only aggregates
body: For the running billion-user app, residency leads to regional partitioning. Each user has a 'home region' where their personal data, such as profile, photos, and messages, is stored. Services that run across regions, such as global analytics or ranking, see only pseudonymized data (identifiers replaced with stand-ins) or aggregated data (counts and statistics). This keeps personal data local by design, so changes in transfer law or new localization rules become configuration changes rather than migrations.
deeper:
Regional partitioning answers several requirements at once. GDPR transfer limits are met by not transferring personal data in the first place. Localization rules like India's RBI payment data rule or China's PIPL are met by assigning users to in-country home regions. Sovereignty goals are easier because each region can have its own keys and operators.

The hard parts are the cross-region features. A user in the EU messaging a user in the US, or a global feed, requires careful design about which region stores what and what crosses boundaries. Pseudonymization and aggregation are the tools: a global service can know that 'user X7' liked a post type without knowing who X7 is.

The chapter's residency lens also applies here. The home region must hold not only primary data but also the logs, indexes, backups, and keys for that user's data, or the partitioning is only partial. Building this early is far cheaper than retrofitting after a fine or a court ruling, as Meta's 2023 order to stop storing EU data in the US showed.

quiz.q: In a home-region design, what may cross-region services see, and why?
quiz.a: Only pseudonymized or aggregated data. That lets global features work without moving identifiable personal data out of the user's home region.

section: 11.2 Certifications and what auditors look for
title: SOC 2: Type I is a snapshot, Type II is a track record
body: Customers, especially enterprises and governments, want independent proof that you are secure. SOC 2 is a report issued by independent CPA firms using AICPA criteria. It covers controls for security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy. A Type I report assesses controls at a single point in time. A Type II report tests that controls actually operated over a period, usually 6 to 12 months. Enterprise buyers generally trust Type II far more, because it proves sustained practice.
deeper:
Typical storage evidence for SOC 2 includes access reviews, encryption settings, backup and restore tests, and change approvals. For a Type II report, the auditor samples across the whole period: were access reviews actually done every quarter, did restore tests actually happen, was every production change approved? A control that exists on paper but was skipped for two months shows up as an exception.

That is why Type II pushes companies toward automation. If encryption is enforced by an organization policy that blocks unencrypted buckets, and evidence is collected by systems, then the answer for every sampled date is the same and easy to produce. If controls rely on people remembering, gaps appear.

SOC 2 is not a certification in the strict sense but an attestation report. Still, it is often the first thing an enterprise customer asks for, and a missing or qualified report can block a sale. For storage teams, the report is where backup testing and access review discipline become visible to customers.

quiz.q: Why do enterprise buyers value a SOC 2 Type II report more than Type I?
quiz.a: Type I only shows controls exist at one moment. Type II tests that controls actually operated over 6 to 12 months, proving sustained practice.

section: 11.2 Certifications and what auditors look for
title: ISO 27001 and FedRAMP: risk systems and federal authorization
body: ISO/IEC 27001 is a certification from accredited certification bodies for an information security management system (ISMS): a managed process for identifying risks and applying Annex A controls. Storage evidence includes a risk register, an asset inventory, and a key management policy. FedRAMP is a US government program that authorizes cloud services for federal agencies, based on NIST SP 800-53 controls at Low, Moderate, or High levels. Storage evidence includes FIPS 140 validated encryption, continuous monitoring, and US-based controls.
deeper:
The two frameworks test different things. ISO 27001 is about the management system: does the organization have a repeatable risk process, does it know its assets, and does it have policies, such as for keys, that it follows? For storage, the asset inventory is non-trivial: you must know which data stores exist and what they hold, which foreshadows the data map discussed later.

FedRAMP is more prescriptive and technical. Its baselines at Low, Moderate, or High impact come from NIST SP 800-53. The encryption requirement is specific: cryptographic modules must be FIPS 140 validated, meaning tested against a US government standard. That is why KMS services run on fleets of FIPS 140 validated HSMs. FedRAMP also expects continuous monitoring, not just a one-time review, and US-based controls, which overlaps with the sovereignty idea of in-country operations.

A provider selling to both enterprises and the US government typically carries SOC 2, ISO 27001, and FedRAMP, and designs storage controls once to satisfy all three.

quiz.q: What specific encryption requirement does FedRAMP add for storage?
quiz.a: Encryption must use FIPS 140 validated cryptographic modules, which is why KMS services run on FIPS 140 validated HSMs.

section: 11.2 Certifications and what auditors look for
title: What storage auditors actually check
body: Across frameworks, auditors check the same things in storage. Encryption at rest and in transit everywhere, FIPS 140 validated for FedRAMP. Key management with separation of duties, so no one person controls both data and keys. Least privilege with regular access reviews. Tamper-resistant logs. Tested restores with evidence, not just backups that exist. Enforced retention and deletion. And traceable configuration changes. If you can prove these continuously, most certifications become a matter of mapping evidence to controls.
deeper:
Each item has a common failure mode. 'Encryption everywhere' fails on the forgotten bucket or the old volume created before defaults changed. 'Separation of duties' fails when the same admin role can read data and manage its KMS keys. 'Access reviews' fail when they are rubber-stamped or skipped. 'Tamper-resistant logs' fail when logs sit in the same account an attacker or insider controls. 'Tested restores' fail when backups exist but nobody has proven a restore works, which auditors specifically ask to see. 'Enforced retention and deletion' fails when policies exist on paper but data lingers in lakes and backups. 'Traceable changes' fails when configuration is edited by hand in a console.

The key takeaway of the chapter condenses this: auditors look for encryption everywhere, key control, least privilege with access reviews, tamper-resistant logs, tested backups, and enforced retention, and you should automate the evidence. Designing storage so these properties are defaults rather than tasks is what makes audits routine.

quiz.q: Why do auditors ask for tested restores rather than just proof that backups exist?
quiz.a: A backup that has never been restored may not work. Evidence of successful restores proves the data can actually be recovered.

section: 11.2 Certifications and what auditors look for
title: Audits aren't yearly projects: continuous compliance
body: A common mistake is treating audits as a yearly project, with a scramble for screenshots before the auditor arrives. Mature companies use continuous compliance. Automated checks, such as AWS Config, Azure Policy, and Google Cloud Organization Policy, catch problems like an unencrypted bucket within minutes, and evidence is collected by systems, not screenshots. Compliance becomes a property that is monitored all year, and the audit becomes an export of evidence that already exists.
deeper:
The yearly-project approach has two problems. First, it hides drift: a bucket created unencrypted in February may stay that way until the audit in November, which is exactly the kind of gap a SOC 2 Type II auditor will find when sampling across the period. Second, manual evidence like screenshots is slow to produce, easy to fake by accident, and does not prove the state on any other day.

Continuous compliance tools evaluate resources against rules as they change. They can alert, auto-remediate (for example, turning on encryption), or, at the organization level, prevent the non-compliant action entirely. Evidence is then a query: show every bucket and its encryption status for each day of the period.

This connects to the chapter's later senior staff lens on preventive guardrails: rules that make mistakes impossible at the organization level scale to tens of thousands of buckets, while dashboards that show mistakes after the fact do not.

quiz.q: Why is screenshot-based evidence weak for a SOC 2 Type II audit?
quiz.a: Type II covers months, but a screenshot proves state at one moment. Automated checks and system-collected evidence show controls held throughout and catch drift in minutes.

title: Encryption at rest: pick the layer by the threat
body: Encryption at rest can happen at several layers, each covering different threats. Self-encrypting disks protect against stolen or discarded drives, but not anyone on the running server. Volume or block encryption (Amazon EBS encryption, Linux dm-crypt) adds protection against snapshot leaks, but not an admin with volume access. Service-side object encryption (S3 SSE-KMS, Google Cloud Storage default) stops storage insiders without key access. Client-side encryption before upload even stops the provider and misconfigured buckets.
deeper:
The rule of thumb: the higher the layer, the more threats it covers, and the more work and risk it puts on you. Each layer also has a clear blind spot. Service-side object encryption does nothing against anyone with IAM rights to read the object, because the service decrypts for them automatically. That is why IAM mistakes, not disk theft, cause most real breaches. Client-side encryption does not protect against bugs in your own app or stolen app credentials, since the app holds the keys.

The costs of high-layer encryption are real. If you lose client-side keys, the data is gone. Search, indexing, and deduplication become hard or impossible, because the storage system sees only ciphertext, and identical plaintexts encrypt to different ciphertexts.

In practice, layers are stacked: drives may be self-encrypting, volumes encrypted, and objects encrypted service-side with customer-managed keys, with client-side encryption reserved for the most sensitive data. Choosing layers starts with the threat model: who are you defending against?

quiz.q: Why doesn't service-side object encryption protect against a principal with IAM read rights?
quiz.a: The storage service decrypts automatically for any authorized reader. The encryption only guards against those without IAM or key access, like disk thieves or storage insiders.

title: S3 and Google encrypt everything by default now
body: Since January 2023, Amazon S3 encrypts all new objects by default with SSE-S3, where the keys are managed by S3 itself. Customers can instead choose SSE-KMS, with keys in AWS KMS, or client-side encryption. Google Cloud encrypts all customer data at rest by default: data is split into chunks, each chunk is encrypted with its own data key, and those keys are wrapped by keys held in Google's key management system. Baseline encryption is now automatic, not a checkbox.
deeper:
Default encryption closes the old failure mode where someone forgot to enable encryption on a bucket. But the choice of key management still matters. With SSE-S3, S3 manages keys internally, which protects against disk theft but gives the customer no separate control point. With SSE-KMS, every decryption goes through AWS KMS, so KMS key policies become a second, independent access gate, and every use is logged. That is what enables customer-managed keys, disabling access by disabling a key, and crypto-shredding.

Google's per-chunk design is envelope encryption at fine granularity. Because each chunk has its own data key, a single leaked data key exposes very little, and the wrapping keys held in the key management system control access to everything.

For architects, defaults mean the question moves from 'is it encrypted?' to 'who controls the keys, and what does that let us do?', which is the subject of the rest of this section.

quiz.q: If S3 already encrypts everything with SSE-S3, why might a team choose SSE-KMS?
quiz.a: SSE-KMS makes KMS key policies a second access gate, logs every key use, and allows customer control like disabling keys or crypto-shredding.

title: Envelope encryption: DEKs encrypt data, KEKs encrypt DEKs
body: You cannot send a 5 GB video to a key management service (KMS) to be encrypted: it would be a huge bottleneck, and the master key would be used for trillions of operations. Envelope encryption solves this. A data encryption key (DEK) is a random key, generated per object, chunk, or file, that encrypts the actual data locally. A key encryption key (KEK), or master key, lives inside the KMS, never leaves it in plain form, and only wraps DEKs. The wrapped DEK is stored next to the data.
deeper:
The write path: the storage service calls KMS GenerateDataKey for KEK k1. KMS, backed by an HSM, returns both a plaintext DEK and the same DEK wrapped under k1. The service encrypts the object with the plaintext DEK, writes the ciphertext and the wrapped DEK to disk, and erases the plaintext DEK from memory.

The read path: the service reads the ciphertext and wrapped DEK, asks KMS to decrypt the wrapped DEK with k1, and KMS returns the plaintext DEK only after an access check. The service then decrypts the object locally.

So the only thing that ever travels to KMS is a small key, not the data. The bulk work, encrypting gigabytes, happens locally at full speed. The master key stays inside hardware and performs only wrap and unwrap operations. Storing the wrapped DEK alongside the data means no separate lookup table is needed: whoever has the ciphertext also has the wrapped key, but cannot use it without KMS permission.

quiz.q: Why is the wrapped DEK safe to store right next to the ciphertext?
quiz.a: It is encrypted under the KEK, which never leaves the KMS. Unwrapping requires an authorized, logged KMS call, so holding the wrapped DEK alone doesn't let anyone decrypt.

title: Why envelope encryption powers access control, rotation, and shredding
body: Envelope encryption gives four big benefits. Bulk encryption is local and fast. Every DEK unwrap is an authorized, logged KMS call, so removing permission on the master key (KEK) blocks reading even if the encrypted bytes leak. Rotating the KEK means re-wrapping small DEKs, not re-encrypting petabytes. And destroying a key makes data unreadable, which is called crypto-shredding. These properties are why envelope encryption is the foundation for nearly every storage security feature in this chapter.
deeper:
The access-control benefit is subtle but important. Normally, if a copy of your storage leaks, for example a snapshot shared by mistake, the data is exposed. With envelope encryption under a KMS key, the attacker also needs permission to call KMS with that key, which they usually do not have. And every unwrap is logged, which helps prove what was or was not read.

There is a cost at very high request rates: even one KMS call per object is expensive. S3 Bucket Keys reduce this by creating a short-lived bucket-level key from KMS and deriving object keys from it, which AWS says can cut KMS request costs substantially. The trade-off is fewer, coarser KMS interactions in exchange for lower cost and load.

The chapter's key takeaway summarizes it: envelope encryption separates fast local data encryption from centrally controlled master keys, making access control, rotation, and crypto-shredding practical.

quiz.q: How do S3 Bucket Keys reduce cost in an envelope encryption system?
quiz.a: They get a short-lived bucket-level key from KMS and derive object keys from it, avoiding one KMS call per object and cutting KMS request costs.

title: Rotating the master key won't save a leaked data key
body: Key rotation means replacing key material on a schedule, to limit how much data one key protects and how long a leaked key stays useful. In AWS KMS, automatic rotation of a customer managed key creates new key material every year by default; the period can be customized, and on-demand rotation is possible. Old material is kept so existing data still decrypts, and KMS picks the right version automatically. Crucially, rotating the KMS key does not re-encrypt data or rotate the data keys.
deeper:
This detail trips up many teams. In envelope encryption, data is encrypted by data keys (DEKs); the master key only wraps them. Rotating the master key means new wraps use new material, and old material stays available to unwrap existing DEKs. The DEKs themselves, and the ciphertext they produced, are unchanged.

So if a data key for one bucket leaks, master key rotation does nothing: the attacker already holds the plaintext DEK and can decrypt that data directly, without KMS. The fix is to re-encrypt the affected data with new data keys and investigate how the leak happened.

What rotation does protect against is a compromise of the master key material over time, and it limits how much newly wrapped data depends on any one version. Rotation is cheap precisely because it avoids touching data, but that same property means it is not a remedy for exposed data keys. The chapter's key takeaway states it plainly: rotating the master key does not re-encrypt data.

quiz.q: Your company rotates its KMS master key yearly, and a data key for one bucket leaks. Does rotation help?
quiz.a: No. Rotation changes only master key material for new wraps; it doesn't change data keys or re-encrypt data. You must re-encrypt with new data keys and investigate.

title: Provider keys vs customer-managed keys vs BYOK
body: Enterprises and regulators often want control of keys, not just encryption. With provider-managed keys, the provider creates and controls keys: easiest, least control. With customer-managed keys (CMK), keys live in the provider's KMS, but the customer controls policies, rotation, disabling, and deletion; disabling the key instantly blocks all access to data encrypted under it. With BYOK (bring your own key), the customer generates key material in its own system and imports it into the provider's KMS, and can delete it from KMS at any time.
deeper:
Each step adds control and responsibility. Customer-managed keys are the common enterprise choice because they give a real off switch without changing how storage works. The provider's services still call their own KMS, so performance and availability stay high, but the customer can revoke access with one action, and all key usage is logged in the customer's account.

BYOK goes further on provenance. Because the customer generated the key material outside the provider, it can prove where the key came from, keep a copy in its own systems, and remove it from the provider's KMS whenever it chooses. That can matter for regulators who want assurance that the provider never created or solely held the key.

The risk grows with control. If a customer deletes a CMK or BYOK key by mistake, the data encrypted under it is unreadable, which is crypto-shredding by accident. Key deletion therefore needs the same review discipline as deleting the data itself.

quiz.q: What does disabling a customer-managed key do, and why is that useful?
quiz.a: It instantly blocks access to all data encrypted under that key, because every decrypt needs KMS to unwrap the data key. It gives the customer a real off switch.

title: HYOK: the key never enters the cloud, and neither does uptime
body: With HYOK (hold your own key), the key never enters the provider at all. The provider must call the customer's external key manager for every unwrap of a data key. Examples are AWS KMS External Key Store (XKS), launched in 2022, and Google Cloud External Key Manager (EKM). The customer can cut off the provider completely, and the provider cannot decrypt without the customer. The cost: if the external key manager is slow or down, your storage is down too.
deeper:
HYOK gives the strongest sovereignty argument. Since the key material never enters the provider, the provider cannot be compelled to decrypt data on its own, and the customer can revoke all access instantly by refusing unwrap calls. That is attractive for regulated industries and for addressing concerns like those raised in Schrems II about foreign government access.

But it moves a critical dependency outside the provider's infrastructure. Every read of encrypted data depends on the customer's key manager being up, fast, and reachable over the network. A slow external key manager adds latency to every unwrap. An outage, a network partition, or a misconfigured firewall between the cloud and the key manager makes data unreadable. The customer now owns an availability problem that used to be the provider's.

The chapter's key takeaway summarizes it: BYOK and HYOK give customers more control but shift availability risk to the key service.

quiz.q: What does HYOK give a customer, and what new risk does it create?
quiz.a: The provider can't decrypt without the customer, who can cut off access anytime. But storage availability now depends on the external key manager and the network to it.

title: Key control trades sovereignty for availability
body: More key control means more sovereignty and less availability. HYOK (hold your own key) puts your storage availability on your own key service: every read waits on it, and every outage of it is a storage outage. For most data, customer-managed keys in the provider's KMS are the right balance: the customer controls policy, rotation, disabling, and deletion, while the provider runs a highly available, HSM-backed service. Reserve HYOK for data where regulators or contracts truly require it.
deeper:
This is a senior staff lens because it frames key choices as a trade-off rather than a maturity ladder. It is tempting to see HYOK as simply 'more secure' and push it everywhere. The cost is that a small, customer-run key service becomes a hard dependency of massive storage systems. Cloud KMS services are built on fleets of FIPS 140 validated HSMs with large-scale redundancy; few customers can match that.

A reasonable policy is tiered. Default data uses provider-managed or customer-managed keys. Sensitive or regulated data uses customer-managed keys with tight key policies and logging. Only data under explicit regulatory or contractual demands, such as sovereignty obligations, uses HYOK, with the external key manager engineered for high availability and low latency.

The same logic appears across the chapter: controls should match real requirements. Over-applying an expensive control, like HYOK or compliance-mode locks, can create outages or irreversible costs that outweigh the risk it addresses.

quiz.q: Why is HYOK not the right default for all data?
quiz.a: It makes storage availability depend on your own key service. Customer-managed keys in the provider's KMS give strong control with far better availability for most data.

title: HSMs: the hardware root of trust under every KMS
body: A hardware security module (HSM) is a tamper-resistant device that stores keys and performs cryptographic operations inside itself, so keys never appear in normal server memory. Key management services (KMS) are built on fleets of FIPS 140 validated HSMs. The root of trust is therefore hardware: the master keys that wrap all data keys live in devices designed to resist physical and logical extraction. Even the provider's own engineers cannot simply copy them out.
deeper:
HSMs matter because the whole envelope encryption model depends on the master key (KEK) staying secret. If a KEK appeared in ordinary server memory, a memory dump, a debugging session, or a compromised host could leak it and expose everything it wraps. By keeping the KEK inside an HSM and exposing only wrap and unwrap operations, the design limits what any software compromise can steal.

FIPS 140 validation is the formal proof that the module meets a US government standard, which is required for FedRAMP and valued by other auditors. That is why the certifications section lists FIPS 140 validated encryption as typical storage evidence.

In the envelope encryption diagram, the KMS is shown as 'KMS with HSM': GenerateDataKey and decrypt calls ultimately execute inside HSMs. The storage service handles only plaintext DEKs briefly in memory and erases them after use, while the long-lived secrets stay in hardware.

quiz.q: Why does it matter that master keys live inside HSMs rather than server memory?
quiz.a: Keys in normal memory can leak via dumps, debugging, or host compromise. HSMs keep keys inside tamper-resistant hardware and expose only crypto operations.

title: Encryption in transit: TLS, mTLS, and ALTS
body: Data must also be protected while moving. TLS (version 1.2 or 1.3) encrypts traffic between clients and services, and storage services can enforce it, for example with an S3 bucket policy that denies requests where aws:SecureTransport is false. mTLS (mutual TLS) also authenticates the client with a certificate; it is standard inside service meshes and between internal services. Google uses its own protocol, ALTS, for service-to-service authentication and encryption inside its network. Major clouds also encrypt traffic between data centers.
deeper:
Enforcement is the key word. Supporting TLS is not the same as requiring it: a misconfigured client could still send data in plaintext if the service allows it. A bucket policy that denies non-TLS requests makes the secure path the only path, which is exactly what auditors want to see when they check 'encryption in transit everywhere'.

mTLS solves a different problem: inside a data center, you want each service to prove its identity, not just encrypt the pipe. With client certificates, a storage service can know which service is calling and apply access rules accordingly. Service meshes automate certificate issuance and rotation so teams do not manage this by hand.

Google's ALTS plays the same role internally, combining authentication and encryption for service-to-service calls. Cross-data-center encryption, often done at the network layer by the major clouds, protects replication traffic between regions, which is where large volumes of user data move for durability and disaster recovery.

quiz.q: How can an S3 bucket enforce encryption in transit, and why enforce rather than just support TLS?
quiz.a: A bucket policy denying requests where aws:SecureTransport is false. Enforcing blocks misconfigured clients from sending plaintext, making TLS the only path.

title: Confidential computing: encrypting data while it's being used
body: Encryption at rest and in transit leave one gap: data in memory during processing. Confidential computing closes it using CPU features such as AMD SEV-SNP and Intel TDX, or enclaves such as AWS Nitro Enclaves, plus remote attestation, which lets a remote party verify exactly what code is running before trusting it with secrets. For storage, it matters mainly for key handling: plaintext keys and data can be processed inside protected memory that even the host operator cannot read.
deeper:
The chapter treats this briefly because storage systems use it narrowly. The main application is protecting the moments when keys or plaintext exist in memory, such as when a service holds a plaintext DEK during encryption. Attestation lets a key service release keys only to code it has verified, which strengthens the chain of trust from HSM to application.

There is an important caveat that links to Chapter 10: confidential computing trusts the CPU even more than ordinary computing does, and CPUs can have silent defects. A CPU that silently computes wrong results could corrupt data or crypto operations inside an enclave, where the extra isolation also makes such errors harder to observe from outside.

So confidential computing is a tool for specific threats, mainly a malicious or compromised host operator, rather than a universal upgrade. It adds complexity, depends on hardware features and attestation infrastructure, and should be weighed against the actual threat model.

quiz.q: What gap does confidential computing close, and what new trust does it require?
quiz.a: It protects data in memory during processing. It requires trusting the CPU even more, and CPUs can have silent defects, as Chapter 10 discusses.

title: One user's data lives in eight kinds of places
body: 'Delete this user's data' sounds like one DELETE statement. At a big company it is one of the hardest distributed-systems problems. In the running app, one user's data sits in primary stores (profile database, photo blob store, message store), replicas (in-region and cross-region), caches (CDN edges, Memcached or Redis, client devices), indexes (search, social graph edges, recommendation features), logs and events (Kafka topics, request and audit logs), derived data (analytics tables, ML training sets), backups, and even other users' data.
deeper:
Each location has its own deletion mechanics. Replicas usually follow the primary, but cross-region replicas may lag or be managed by another team. Caches need invalidation, and client devices may hold copies you cannot directly delete. Indexes must be updated or rebuilt so the user no longer appears in search or recommendations. Kafka topics and logs are append-only, so deletion usually means waiting for retention to expire or rewriting segments. Derived data like analytics tables and ML training sets may mix the user's data with others', so removal can mean rewriting files or retraining. Backups and snapshots are often immutable by design.

The 'other users' data' case is the trickiest conceptually: a comment you left on someone else's photo belongs partly to you and partly to their content. Should it disappear? That is a product and legal decision that must be encoded.

A central deletion framework handles this by fanning a request for, say, user 42 out to handlers for every store, including profile rows, photos, graph edges and comments, indexes, caches and CDN, logs and the analytics lake, and backups (expire or crypto-shred), and then verifying and recording completion.

quiz.q: After a user's profile row is deleted, name five places their data may still exist.
quiz.a: Cross-region replicas, caches and CDN, search and graph indexes, Kafka topics and request logs, the analytics lake and ML sets, backups and snapshots, and comments on others' content.

title: Graphs, Parquet files, backups, drift: why deletion breaks
body: Four specific problems make deletion hard. Graph deletion: when a photo is deleted, should its comments and likes go too? Immutable lake files: deleting one row rewrites whole Parquet files, even with Iceberg, Delta, or Hudi delete files. Backups: you expire them rather than rewrite them, and must re-apply deletes after any restore. Drift: new tables that nobody added to the deletion logic. Each can leave data behind silently, which is exactly what auditors and regulators look for.
deeper:
Graph deletion is about semantics. Some edges are ownership (a photo owns its comments), others are references to other users (a friend link). Cascading along the wrong edge deletes someone else's data; not cascading along the right one leaves orphans.

Lake formats store data in large immutable columnar files. Table formats like Iceberg, Delta, and Hudi can record delete files that mark rows as removed, but the underlying bytes remain until files are rewritten or compacted. Deleting scattered users across a huge table can mean rewriting much of it.

Backups are immutable for good reason, so rewriting them per request is impractical. The approach is to let them expire on a schedule, and, critically, to replay deletions after any restore so a deleted user does not come back. Crypto-shredding offers another route.

Drift is organizational: engineers add new tables and pipelines constantly. If deletion logic is a separate list someone must update, it will fall behind. DELF's answer is to make deletion behavior part of the schema.

quiz.q: Why must deletions be re-applied after restoring from a backup?
quiz.a: Backups are expired, not rewritten, so they still contain users deleted after the backup was taken. Restoring without replaying deletions would bring those users' data back.

title: Meta's DELF: deletion behavior declared in the schema
body: Meta (then Facebook) published DELF at USENIX Security 2020 (Cohn-Gordon et al.). The problem: developers must translate 'delete this account' into precise operations on many data types, and mistakes either leave data behind or delete the wrong data. With DELF, developers annotate each data type and each edge in the schema with deletion behavior, such as 'when the parent is deleted, delete this too', or 'this is a link to another user, do not cascade'.
deeper:
DELF then runs deletions as asynchronous, reliable, and temporarily reversible operations across backing data stores. Asynchronous and reliable matter because a single account deletion can touch enormous numbers of objects across many systems, so it must survive failures and retries rather than run as one transaction. Temporarily reversible matters because mistakes happen.

DELF also performs static and dynamic validation to catch missing or wrong annotations. Static checks look at the schema: is every type and edge annotated, and are the annotations consistent? Dynamic checks observe real deletions to find cases where data that should have been deleted was not, or vice versa.

The results were substantial. The paper reports that, across three social networks, DELF detected thousands of omissions, corrected dozens of mistakes, and helped recover from tens of incidents where data was deleted by mistake. That shows both failure directions are real at scale: leaving data behind and deleting too much.

quiz.q: How does DELF distinguish between edges that should cascade a delete and ones that shouldn't?
quiz.a: Developers annotate each edge in the schema, e.g. 'delete with parent' for owned data vs 'link to another user, do not cascade', and DELF enforces and validates those annotations.

title: Two DELF ideas to copy: schema-declared and briefly reversible
body: Two ideas from Meta's DELF deletion system are worth copying. First, make deletion behavior part of the schema. If a new table cannot be created without declaring how it is deleted, you cannot forget it, which eliminates drift. Second, make deletion reversible for a short time. Mistaken deletions happen, for example a bug deletes the wrong edges. DELF keeps restoration logs for a limited period so it can undo them, and after that the data is gone for good.
deeper:
The first idea turns a process problem into a type-system problem. Instead of relying on engineers to update a deletion script whenever they add a table, the platform refuses to create the table until its deletion behavior is declared. That is the chapter's 'make the safe path the easy path' principle applied to deletion.

The second idea addresses the opposite risk. Privacy teams naturally focus on leaving data behind, but at Meta's scale, deleting the wrong data is also an incident. DELF helped recover from tens of such incidents. A time-limited restoration log gives a safety window without undermining the privacy goal, because the window is bounded and the log itself is deleted afterward.

This mirrors other systems in the chapter. Google Cloud's deletion pipeline includes a soft-delete recovery period of up to about 30 days before logical deletion. The pattern is the same: a short, bounded undo period, then permanent removal within a published deadline.

quiz.q: Why is it acceptable under privacy goals for DELF to keep restoration logs?
quiz.a: They exist only for a limited period to undo mistaken deletions. After the window, the logs and data are gone for good, so erasure still completes.

title: Crypto-shredding: delete the key, not the data
body: Crypto-shredding, or cryptographic erasure, means encrypting data with a key and later deleting the key instead of the data. Without the key, the ciphertext is useless. This solves the hardest deletion cases. Backups: if a user's data is encrypted with a per-user key, deleting that key 'deletes' the user from every backup at once, without rewriting any. Many copies: replicas, on-disk caches, and logs all become unreadable together. Immutable storage: data you cannot rewrite can still be made unreadable.
deeper:
The costs are real. You may need a very large number of keys, possibly one per user, which means a key store that handles huge scale. That key store becomes critical: lose it and you lose everything, so it needs strong durability and availability. You must prove the key is gone from every key backup, since a surviving copy of the key would undo the erasure. And you must choose the right key granularity from the start: if data was encrypted per dataset, you cannot shred one user's records without re-encrypting.

Crypto-shredding is why envelope encryption and per-user or per-dataset keys appear in the chapter's list of platform building blocks. It is especially valuable for backups, which are immutable by design and otherwise must be expired on long cycles.

Cloud providers use it directly. Google Cloud lists cryptographic erasure as one way data is logically deleted from active systems, and Cloud Storage deletes data this way too.

quiz.q: Why must you choose key granularity at the start when planning crypto-shredding?
quiz.a: You can only shred what a key uniquely protects. If data was encrypted per dataset rather than per user, deleting one user's data by key would require re-encrypting everything.

title: Google Cloud's four-stage deletion: up to about 180 days
body: Google Cloud describes its deletion pipeline in four stages. First, the deletion request. Second, a soft-delete recovery period of up to about 30 days. Third, logical deletion from active systems, through garbage collection or cryptographic erasure, which generally takes about two months. Fourth, expiration from backups, which are retired on daily, weekly, and monthly cycles. Google commits to deleting customer data within a maximum of about six months (180 days). In Cloud Storage, data is also deleted through cryptographic erasure.
deeper:
The staged design shows how real systems balance competing needs. The soft-delete period protects against mistakes, similar to DELF's temporary reversibility. Logical deletion from active systems is where most copies disappear, but it still takes around two months because garbage collection and compaction run in the background across large distributed systems. Backups are the long tail: they are not rewritten per request but aged out on their normal daily, weekly, and monthly cycles.

Publishing the 180-day maximum is itself important. Laws usually say 'without undue delay' rather than giving a number, so a company must define and defend its own deadline. A clear public commitment, with each stage accounted for, is what regulators and customers can check against.

The design also demonstrates why crypto-shredding is attractive: destroying keys can make data unreadable across many systems sooner than waiting for every physical copy to be garbage collected.

quiz.q: Why does Google's deletion take up to about 180 days rather than immediately?
quiz.a: It includes a ~30-day soft-delete recovery window, ~two months of logical deletion via garbage collection or crypto-erasure, and backup expiry on daily, weekly, and monthly cycles.

title: Deletion SLAs: the last copy has a deadline
body: A deletion SLA is the maximum time from a deletion request to complete removal, including every copy. Laws usually say 'without undue delay' rather than a number, so companies set their own and publish them. Google Cloud's is about 180 days including backups. Meta's help pages have said that deleting a Facebook account can take up to 90 days, with copies in backup storage possibly lasting longer for disaster recovery. An SLA turns a vague legal duty into a measurable engineering target.
deeper:
To meet an SLA, the deletion system needs four things. A registry of every data store that holds user data, which is the data map described in Section 11.8. Per-store deletion handlers, each with its own completion signal, so the framework knows when each store is done. Tracking and alerting on requests that are stuck, since a single failed handler can silently break the deadline. And verification: sampling or scanning to prove deleted data is really gone, not just marked.

The verification step is what separates a real SLA from a hopeful one. A handler reporting success does not prove there are no stray copies in a forgotten table. Scanning for the deleted user's identifiers across stores gives evidence.

The Meta example highlights the backup nuance: primary deletion within 90 days, while backups for disaster recovery may last longer. An honest SLA states how backups are handled, whether by expiry schedules or crypto-shredding.

quiz.q: What four capabilities does a deletion system need to meet an SLA?
quiz.a: A registry of every store with user data, per-store handlers with completion signals, tracking and alerting on stuck requests, and verification that data is really gone.

title: Deleting the primary row is not deleting the user
body: A common mistake is deleting from the primary database and considering the job done. Auditors and regulators ask about logs, analytics copies, ML training data, and backups. The primary row is usually the easiest copy to remove and the least likely to be the one that causes trouble. If you cannot answer 'when will the last copy be gone?', you do not have a deletion SLA. You have a partial deletion and an unknown amount of residual personal data.
deeper:
The mistake is natural because the primary database is what engineers see and test. A delete endpoint that removes the profile row looks correct in every unit test. But the user's data also lives in Kafka topics, request logs, search indexes, feature stores, the analytics lake, ML training sets, and backups, most of which are owned by other teams.

The question 'when will the last copy be gone?' is a useful test. Answering it requires knowing every store (a data map), knowing each store's deletion mechanism and timing (handlers and retention), and knowing how backups are handled (expiry or crypto-shredding). If any piece is unknown, the honest answer is 'we don't know'.

Regulators treat residual copies seriously because they are exactly where data leaks and misuse happen: an old analytics export or a forgotten training set can be breached years later. The remedy is the full deletion framework described in this section, with verification.

quiz.q: What question tests whether a company really has a deletion SLA?
quiz.a: 'When will the last copy be gone?' If you can't answer for logs, analytics, ML data, and backups, you don't have a deletion SLA.

title: Retention, legal hold, WORM: the keep-it side of the law
body: Deletion and retention pull in opposite directions. Privacy law says delete when no longer needed; financial, tax, and litigation rules say keep and do not touch. A retention policy says how long each data type is kept, for example request logs 30 days, invoices 7 years, broker-dealer records 6 years. A legal hold suspends deletion for data related to a lawsuit or investigation, for as long as the hold lasts, regardless of the normal policy. WORM storage prevents alteration or deletion during retention, even by admins.
deeper:
These three tools work at different levels. Retention policies are the default lifecycle: they drive automatic expiry for privacy (short retention for logs) and guaranteed preservation for regulation (long retention for invoices). They should be declared per data type, ideally in the data map, so both deletion and preservation are automatic.
